passage:
At nine, Harish noticed something: every day he wore his red shirt, his cricket team won. His sister Minakshi laughed when he refused to wash it before the final. "The shirt is why we win," he said, with a straight face. She asked, "What about the day we won when you wore blue?" Harish frowned. He hadn't thought of that.

At fifteen, he saw that students who joined tuition classes scored more in the unit tests, and told his father he needed tuition. His classmate Yamini said, "The ones who go to tuition also do their homework early and have quiet study rooms. Maybe tuition isn't the only reason."

At twenty, in the college canteen, he read a headline claiming that people who drink coffee tend to live longer, and started buying a large cup every morning. Yamini looked at the article with him. "Does it say coffee causes it? Maybe healthier, richer people just drink more of it. Or people who are already ill drink less." Harish pushed the cup aside and kept reading.

qa.q: What colour was the shirt Harish thought brought his team luck?
What thinking mistake does Harish make at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine Harish links the red shirt to wins, at fifteen tuition to higher scores and at twenty coffee to a longer life, each time deciding that one thing causes the other without asking what else might explain both.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when Minakshi asked about the day they won in blue?
qa.a: Harish was puzzled and a little caught out, because he had not thought of that day, and he frowned.

qa.q: What could Harish ask himself the next time a headline links two things?
qa.a: He could ask whether something else, such as health or money, might explain both, or whether the link runs the other way, as Yamini suggested.

grounding: Correlation versus causation at three ages: a child's lucky shirt, a teenager crediting tuition for marks, and a student trusting a coffee headline.
